analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes FAA programs while shifting air traffic control to a corporation governed by aviation-industry nominees.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill 32-25 and placed it on the House calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill does two very different things. It reauthorizes Federal Aviation Administration programs for six years and adds real consumer and safety rules: guaranteed rest for flight attendants, minimum seat dimensions, secondary cockpit barriers, a one-page summary of passenger rights, and customer service standards for large ticket agents. But its centerpiece is a structural overhaul: on October 1, 2020, air traffic control would move out of the FAA and into a new federally chartered, not-for-profit corporation whose board is nominated mostly by panels representing passenger airlines, cargo carriers, regional carriers, business aviation, airports, and pilots.
analysis.who_benefits: Fliers gain new protections (guaranteed flight-attendant rest, secondary cockpit barriers, minimum seat dimensions, a standardized passenger-rights document, customer service standards for large ticket agents, and higher denied-boarding compensation rules). Small and rural communities keep Essential Air Service subsidies. Residents near airports gain noise studies and mitigation grants. Large passenger airlines gain the most unusual benefit: a board seat and a panel that nominates directors of the new corporation that would run air traffic control and set its fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fliers, small communities, and large airlines

how_it_helps.text: Requires flight attendants scheduled for duty periods of 14 hours or less to receive a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours that cannot be reduced under any circumstances.
Directs the FAA to set minimum dimensions for passenger seats on aircraft operated by air carriers and to require secondary cockpit barriers on newly manufactured passenger aircraft.

Requires each air carrier to submit a one-page document describing passengers' rights, requires large ticket agents to adopt minimum customer service standards, and addresses compensation for passengers involuntarily bumped after boarding.

Reauthorizes the Essential Air Service program, which subsidizes flights to small and rural communities, and creates a regional air transportation pilot program for communities with insufficient air service.

Directs a study of the health impacts of aircraft overflight noise and creates a pilot grant program for environmental mitigation projects reducing aviation noise, air quality, or water quality impacts near airports.
Requires medium and large hub airports receiving federal grants to maintain a private lactation room in the sterile area of each terminal.

analysis.who_pays: Travelers and general aviation would fund the new system. The corporation is barred from receiving federal funds and would set its own charges for air traffic services, so the cost of running air traffic control would shift onto users of the system. Airport passenger facility charges could rise from $3 to $4.50 per boarding. General aviation and business aircraft owners, who would have no seats on the board, would pay those fees too. If the transition went badly, taxpayers and fliers would bear the consequences, because the government is expressly not liable for the corporation's actions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fliers, general aviation, and cargo users

drawbacks.text: The corporation is expressly not a government agency, is not subject to federal fiscal law (title 31), and the United States government is not liable for its actions or inactions.

Only 2 of the 13 directors on the board are appointed by the Secretary of Transportation; the rest are nominated by panels representing passenger carriers, cargo carriers, regional carriers, business aviation, general aviation, airports, controllers, and pilots, with the largest airlines each designating a representative to the passenger-carrier panel.

The corporation sets its own charges and fees for air traffic services and is prohibited from receiving federal funds, so the full cost of the system would be carried by the people and businesses that fly.
Airport passenger facility charges could rise from $3 to $4.50 per passenger boarding, and the nonhub pilot program for those charges is expanded.

A transfer of air traffic control from a federal agency to a new corporation is an untested reorganization of a safety-critical system, with the transition scheduled to occur all at once on October 1, 2020.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer, safety, and worker provisions are real and worthwhile, and nothing in the record suggests they depended on the corporatization plan; they could have been enacted on their own. The price of the package was the governance transfer: a system funded by taxpayers and ticket taxes would become one funded and governed primarily by aviation industry panels. Members of Congress who were prepared to vote for the reauthorization apparently judged that trade not worth it, since the bill never reached the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee on a 32-25 vote and was placed on the House calendar, but it was never brought up for a floor vote, and the Congress ended without one.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Shuster introduced the bill on June 22, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The committee ordered the bill reported on June 27, 2017 by a vote of 32 to 25, and reported it as amended on September 6, 2017 (H. Rept. 115-296).
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 213) on September 6, 2017, meaning it was eligible for floor consideration.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a House floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill's stated centerpiece was to transfer operation of air traffic services from the FAA to the American Air Navigation Services Corporation, a federally chartered not-for-profit, on October 1, 2020.
The bill carried 22 cosponsors: 19 Republicans and 3 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the governance transfer — general aviation operators, the air traffic controllers' union, and members of Congress who wanted air traffic control to stay inside the federal government — kept the status quo, and the largest airlines never got their industry-run corporation. The bill's consumer and safety provisions were not lost with it; Congress enacted a separate FAA reauthorization in 2018 that included them. Fliers came out roughly even.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General aviation, controllers, and consumer advocates

for.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, managed it through committee markup, and steered it to a 32-25 committee vote reporting it to the House floor calendar.

for.name: President Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Publicly proposed and urged moving air traffic control out of the FAA into a self-funding corporation during 2017.

for.name: 19 House Republican cosponsors and 3 Democratic cosponsors

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor after it was placed on the Union Calendar.

against.name: National Air Traffic Controllers Association
against.role: Union representing FAA air traffic controllers
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against corporatizing air traffic control, arguing it jeopardized the federal safety workforce.

against.name: General aviation groups (Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association, National Business Aviation Association)
against.role: Trade associations for private and business aircraft owners
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's air traffic control corporation, warning of new fees and loss of access for their members.

against.name: 25 members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee members voting against reporting the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported out of committee, 32-25.

sides.party_line_note: Support skewed Republican: 19 of 22 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee reported the bill 32-25; the provided record does not break down that vote by party.

industries.industry: Large passenger airlines (carriers with over 30 million annual boardings)
industries.note: Each of these carriers would have designated a representative to the panel that nominates a director of the new air traffic services corporation, giving them a governing voice in a service they buy and their customers use. Supporters promised modernization; critics noted the board would answer to industry panels rather than the public.

industries.industry: General aviation and business aircraft owners
industries.note: They would pay the corporation's user fees for air traffic services while holding at most one board seat among thirteen. Their interest in keeping air traffic control publicly accountable ran alongside fliers' interest in the same thing.

Federal air traffic control facilities, personnel, and jobs would be transferred out of government employment to the corporation on the transfer date. The union's fight to stay in federal service aligned with keeping the safety system publicly accountable.
Airports could raise passenger facility charges from $3 to $4.50 per boarding and would gain noise mitigation grants and expanded grant programs, funded by the travelers passing through.
Large all-cargo carriers would also have designated a representative to a nomination panel for the corporation's board, gaining governing influence over the service they depend on.
